title: 34. The benefits of nature, adventure, and connection feat. Brittany Crane (founder of Get Out There Girl)
description_html: Brittany Crane is the author of the highly-praised Self Compassion Workbook - a 15 day guide and journal experience to help you build inner strength, accept yourself and thrive at lifeand the founder and CEO of Get Out There Girl. She is on a mission to help women thrive at life by... connecting with nature through high-adventure retreats, connecting with themselves through self compassion, and connecting with other women through vulnerability. Brittany helps women uncover their critical voices and treat themselves like they would treat a good friend. She believes that self compassion is the tool that will free women from the traps of comparison, guilt, and perfectionism.

paragraphs.text: Welcome to Nevertheless, She Persisted. I'm your host, Sadie. Every Friday, I post interviews about mental health, dialectical behavioral therapy, and teenage life. These episodes break down my mental health journey, teach skills to help you cope with life, and showcase testimonials from teens just like you. Whether you've struggled yourself or just want to improve your mental fitness, this podcast is your inspiration to live a life you love and keep persisting.

This week on She Persisted. My kids are the reason why I prioritize my mental health. I couldn't get past the love that I had for them and how much they deserve that in their life. It just fosters more empowerment because you are the one taking control of your mental health. I've given myself permission to be more compassionate to myself. I've also grown in compassion towards others. Today's guest is Brittany Crane.

the CEO and founder of Get Out There Girl, and the author of the highly praised Self-Compassion Workbook, a 15-day guide and journal experience to help you build inner strength, accept yourself, and thrive at life. Brittany helps women uncover their critical voices and treat themselves like they would treat a good friend. She believes that self-compassion is the tool that will free women from the traps of comparison, guilt, and perfectionism. Brittany is on a mission to help women thrive at life by connecting with nature through high adventure retreats, connecting with themselves through self-compassion, and connecting with other women through vulnerability on Get Out There Girl. Let's get into it.

Thank you so much for joining me today and being open to record with me. Thanks for having me. So I wanted to start this episode the way I start most episodes, which is hearing the mental health story of the guest so that listeners can have an understanding of who they're listening to, what they went through. So can you tell me your mental health journey and kind of what that was like for you? Yeah. So I guess as a teenager, I was kind of always a pessimist. It was easy for me to get sad and depressed. And then...

I changed some life circumstances and got a hold of my mental health and found a lot of joy and happiness. Depression didn't really come back at all until I had my third baby. After I had my third baby, I kind of call it the perfect storm where I moved across the country. I didn't have a support system. My husband started a new career that was really demanding. And then we also opened up a gym, which we were really ambitious, overly ambitious.

But my hormones were all over the place in conjunction with all of that. And after having her, it just things kind of sunk for me. I got really depressed. I had suicidal thoughts and I, I just, I was functioning barely every day. I had my kids to take care of every day, but I was, I was a mess. I cried a lot. I didn't have any motivation. I just thought the world would actually be better without me is what down to. When I shared those thoughts with my husband, he was really surprised. He has never dealt with depression and nobody in his family dealt with depression. So it was all really new to him.

And he encouraged me to go see a counselor. He's like, I have no idea what to do or what to tell you. You should go see somebody who can help. And so I did. I went and saw a counselor and she started validating my thoughts and teaching me tools that would help me with depression and to fight that. Most of all, she taught me that my mind was a muscle and just like I could exercise my body.

and get fit. I could also do that same thing with my mind. I thought that, you know, genetically, I was predetermined to just be sad all the time. And it was something that I couldn't change. But my counselor, Joan, told me that I could. And that was like this big aha moment for me where I was like, wait, I can, you know, I can get in shape and run a half marathon. I can also take charge of my mental health. I'm not doomed to be sad all the time. I can do this.

I love that. I remember the same thing. And I definitely did relate to what you said about how your husband, he didn't understand what to do or know how to go forward. And I think that's where my parents were at as well. I talk about this a lot, but with my dad, especially. So his dad had bipolar. So he's been aware of mental health and depression.

But still, the idea that a kid could experience depression, he was like, no, wait, what? Like, he just didn't know that. And so that is always such a shock for me that even people who have been aware of mental health or mental illness, the thought of kids experiencing it or people experiencing it at a young age, there's just such a lack of education about how you can take control of your mental health and the fact that it can change.

And it's hard to explain to other people. Like I can't imagine trying to think, okay, this is what this depression is feeling like for me because it's so hard to get someone to understand if they haven't been through it. I recorded an episode a couple weeks ago and what I really touched on was like the most difficult part of struggling with a mental illness is how abstract it is.

And that's what gives it the most power at the beginning, because you have no idea what you're up against. And that's why it's so hard to explain to people, because even you don't get it. And it's so subjective with every single different person you come in contact to, which is why there's no roadmap. Like when you go and get treatment for...

The cold, the flu, you present a little bit differently, but there's still a treatment plan that's pretty effective. With mental health, it's so subjective and so different. So it just gives that abstractness even more power. But not to say there's not things you can do to change that. It just takes more work and it's on you. It's on you to figure out what works. It's on you to take ownership of that and you to make those changes. Yeah.

Yeah, I love that. So this next question is a little bit heavy, but I feel like it would be applicable to many listeners, even if they haven't experienced postpartum. So I haven't experienced it myself, but I have struggled with depression. And so for me, that was isolating. That was pushing away my siblings, my friends, my family members.

As a mother, you mentioned you had to take care of your kids while going through this depression. And so I was wondering, like, I can't imagine how much pressure that puts on yourself to recover because you have these other people who are looking to you for care and love and support. And you're like, well, I got to work on me as well. So I was wondering how are you able to prioritize your own mental health and your own recovery while also having others who are looking for you to support them in their lives as well? Yeah. So that's a great question. And that's actually my kids are the reason why I prioritize my mental health.

They need me. And I knew that the level that I was functioning at wasn't long-term. I was just doing the bare minimum and they needed me at my best. They deserved, they deserved a good mom and they, they deserved me. And, and so I got help. Like I said, my husband encouraged me to get that help. And so I would go to counseling weekly. Um,

And then I had, you know, my journaling every day and the different tasks that I did every day. And that was my me time. That was my self-care during that time where I was like, okay, guys, like I need, whether I put on a movie for them or they played with friends or whatever they did. That was, that was time that I spent on me so that I could become a better mom for them. As I thought about it.

Their lives without me, that's what motivated me to change. Because, let's see, I get so emotional when I think about this. Because when I thought about my kids, what their lives would be like if I followed through with suicide... It made me so sad because I knew I was in a dark place and I knew that I wasn't happy and I wasn't sad. And I knew I wasn't the mom that I needed to be at that time. But I also knew that nobody else was going to love my kids the way that I could love them and the way that I love them. Yeah. And so that thought alone was what kept me from following through with my suicidal thoughts. My kids are...

the motivator to not only get healthy, but to also stay alive. I knew that they needed me and they deserved me. And even with all of my deep, dark thoughts, I couldn't get past the love that I had for them and how much they deserve that in their life. I love that. And I think that's something that people get confused about so often is that you want to go and support those around you and help those around you. And we prioritize other people over ourselves sometimes. And it's hard to remember that.

you won't be able to support others. You won't be able to be your best self and give them all of you until you focus on yourself first. And it's like when you get on the airplane and they're like, don't put an oxygen mask on your kid before you do it for yourself. And I'm not a parent, but I imagine that you'd be like, no, I want to help my kid first. Like you put their wellbeing above your own and that's your first instinct.

And yet if you aren't breathing, you have no oxygen, you're no good to the kid and they're going to suffer too. And so I think you can serve others so much more when you're at your strongest and when you are taking care of your mental health. And I think that's something that's hard to remember because especially for me, I struggle with...

for a while with self-esteem and prioritizing myself and believing that I deserved happiness and love and care. And so I didn't want that for myself. I didn't want to invest my mental health or invest in my wellbeing. And yet I wanted to help other people and to really help other people, I needed to work on myself first. And so it's, can you exercise that self-compassion for yourself that will serve others so much more? I think that's my biggest takeaway the past six years. So it's been six years since I,

went through this postpartum depression. And I think that's the biggest takeaway that I've learned is that self-care isn't selfish, that I take care of me so that I have more of me to give. And whether you're a mom or a friend or a sister or a daughter, it doesn't matter. If you put more into yourself, then you'll have more to give out.

Totally. So let's talk Get Out There Girl. So I absolutely love what you're doing with your company. And so I wanted to ask you, what inspired you to start Get Out There Girl? And what's your mission for the organization? So here's how it started. So after my third baby and my experience that I just walked you through with that, I was surprise pregnant with number four. I knew I wanted to have another baby, but he came much sooner than I was expecting. And I was terrified to get depressed again. I had just pulled out of it. And I really didn't want to go back there.

And so for the first two months of my pregnancy with him, I cried. I cried a lot because I was so scared. It wasn't because I didn't want him or I didn't love him. It was just because I was so scared of getting depressed again. Yes. But I kept using all of my tools that my counselor had taught me and everything. And three weeks after he was born, we decided to take a spontaneous trip to Moab. He was tiny, like so tiny, three weeks old. Yeah. But we went and while we were driving, I had this experience that changed my life forever. It's still so vivid in my mind. While we were driving, I had this experience where God literally told me that I had one life and I needed to live it, that I needed to go out and play.

And it was very specific like that. And I love the outdoors. I love going on hikes. I love adventuring. And so at that moment, it was just like this impact where I was like, I need to go out and do things that I love that make me feel alive. And so from that moment on, I put myself back on the priority list and I started doing things that made me happy and that made me feel alive.

And I started inviting friends on those adventures and those hikes. And then they invited their friends and then they invited their friends. And then I had strangers coming with me. And so I always knew what adventure and getting outside did for my mental health. But then I watched it happen to dozens of other women. And I was like, wait, I think I have something here. It's not just me. This works for a lot.

Yeah, there's there's a recipe here. And so after a year of doing that and seeing it happen over and over again, I made it official and created Get Out There Girl. And so Get Out There Girl has a threefold mission. It's to empower women through adventure, self-compassion and making connections. Those are the three things that I think women need to thrive.

So our goal is to help women rediscover their worth while adventuring out nature. And we do a workshop on each retreat, some type of self-education, whether that's on resilience or self-compassion, or we just did a retreat and the workshop was mind body bridging, which was fascinating. So there's all of these different educational things that we can learn about our mental health while we're on this retreat and,

And then women just come alive. They make connections with a dozen other women and they go home better than they came. And it's magic for me to watch. I love coming home from Eat Treat Treat and just witnessing the changes that happen in all of these women. That's amazing. I love that. So there's so many directions that you could have gone with.

Get out there, girl, whether it was like just the educational part with working on your mental fitness. So I wanted to ask you why outdoor exercise and adventure as the core of this program? Well, mostly because I experienced it myself. I knew what worked for me. But... As I studied, I realized why those work so well. Both adventure and self-compassion have been proven to relieve stress, anxiety, and depression. Moving your body creates endorphins and serotonin, which help increase your happiness. And then studies, I've been researching fresh air lately, and they've shown that fresh air, the oxygen combined with the smells, they actually increase your energy

And then on top of all that, you get vitamin D, which helps your mood too, right? Yeah. So studies have shown it. But then for me personally, it's easy for me to get more depressed when I'm inside, when I'm isolated. Totally. And I just kind of let my mind run away with myself. a negative place. But when I go outside, I can control my negativity better. I take more deep breaths. I'm more mindful and aware. I'm able to see the good in the world by witnessing, you know, how beautiful the earth is. And I also put my problems into perspective. I connect with other people. I hear their stories. I see their struggles. And then I'm, I can focus on our shared humanity, how we all go through hard things and we all struggle. It's not just me. I'm not

really isolated. That was just a mindset that I had. And so combining all of those things, make it, make it work for me. Uh, yeah. Also the adventure side of it, a little bit of adrenaline goes a long way. There's a term that some people call flow and flow in this sense refers to finding the sweet spot of going just outside your comfort zone, but not going into fight or flight mode. Yeah.

Yes. And so this flow or sweet spot creates an amazing feeling of empowerment. So women come on these rappelling trips with me and they get to experience that flow. They come alive. And it's one of my favorite things to watch. They do something just outside of their comfort zone where they're like, oh my gosh, am I really doing this? Yeah, let's go. Let's do this. And then they rappel off a cliff and it's...

It's this amazing experience. It also forces you to focus on the present and live in the moment, which is great practice for everyday life because you can't be thinking about your to-do list or you can't be thinking about what a terrible person you are while you're repelling off a cliff. You've got to focus and you're just in the moment and it's adrenaline filling and it's...

happy fit like serotonin and endorphins firing. And you've got other women who are encouraging you along the way. It's, it's really just magic. Yeah, no, I remember the same thing. I've talked about this somewhat on the podcast, but a huge part of the therapeutic boarding school program that I was at was they called it adventure. And so it was every Friday and Saturday, all the girls on campus, we would go and during the winter, it was skiing and snowboarding. And then during the summer, it was rock climbing or mountain biking or hiking and we'd go rafting and stuff like that. And so it was the same things. And it was, it helped so many girls because again, getting out,

Even from a depression standpoint, it does wonders for your mental health. And then you're building these connections. You're showing yourself that you have power, you can do these things, and you're taking your mind off what seems all-consuming. And so I know that was huge for me in my journey. And I really do love the way that you're approaching it because...

When we were at therapeutic boarding school, of course, there was girls that didn't want to go hiking every single weekend and then refused to go. And a lot of the time it was like you're being forced to do it. Of course, there's still benefits to being outside, but there's something about being empowered to do it yourself and seeking that out on your own. I feel like it just fosters such stronger connections and more empowerment because it's all on you and you are the one taking control of your mental health. So I love that you're making that available.

And letting people like choose to do that themselves rather than the boarding school perspective where I was like, oh, you got to go or like there was a consequence. But I love that you're implementing those same principles and for all ages, too. Like that's so, so, so cool. Yeah, and I found that women want to be there and they want to make connections. They want new friendships. And so that just makes it even better because then you have, you know, a dozen women coming together who want to be there. They want to.

to be your friend. They want to hear your story and they're willing to be vulnerable with theirs. And so it just makes the connections genuine and sincere. And then people go, with a dozen new friends that they stay in touch with and they connected with on a deep level. Totally. And it's like this idea that we not only attract those that are kind of giving off, like, I don't know if energy would be the right term, but like have the same mindset as us. And so when all these people are here and they're motivated to improve themselves and work on their mental health and build connections, it's just a stronger, more enjoyable experience for everyone. And so I love that for sure.

So when I talked to you before our recording, we touched a little bit on vulnerability as a component of retreat. So I wanted to ask you why you built this into the Get Out Girl initiative in addition to the adventure and exercise component. Well, vulnerability actually came naturally as I shared my story. I hate the negative stigma around mental health disorders and

Never want anybody to feel as alone as I did. And so I started sharing my experience. I was very open with it and I didn't try to hide anything. And I noticed that as I shared, then other women were more open and vulnerable with me. It just takes a slight opening of the door for somebody who's looking for it and longing for it. Yeah. To grasp a hold of it and take it. And that's what I found. I found women want to be vulnerable. Women want to be real. And they don't want to hide. And they want to share all of their story, the good and the bad. And if you give them that opportunity by sharing your good and your bad, then they're more willing. They feel safe.

and they're open up to, but I actually created a blog series called share my story where every Monday I share a different woman's story where she blogs about her experience of overcoming or healing from something that she's been struggling with, with one of the three pillars of get out there girl. So adventure, self-compassion or making connections. She shares how she's struggling with something and how she's overcoming it with, with,

with one of those three things. And one of my favorite parts of that is to read the comments from other women who read it and say something like, oh my gosh, I had no idea that that's something that you struggle with. I do too. We should get together and talk or I'm going to message you. Women tell me, hey, I've made a new friend today because I shared my story on your blog or different things like that, that it makes my heart really happy. And it's just an avenue, I think, for women to share. And it needs we need to share. We need to be real with our stories and stop hiding because there are so many people out there who need us and who need to hear our stories in order to share their own.

Yeah, I love it. You put it perfectly. So digging more into the idea of vulnerability and self-compassion and all of that. So again, self-compassion is a big part of the Get Out Girl mission. So I wanted to know how has self-compassion helped you personally and then a little bit more like the vulnerability. How have you seen it impact others that have participated in the Get Out Girl program? Oh, gosh. Self-compassion has been such a life changer for me.

It's freed me from shame, shame that I'm not a valuable person, shame that I'm not a good mother or a good wife, shame that other people are better than I am. Self-compassion has given me the permission to set high goals and then become the best version of me. I've always been so critical of myself. I always looked for ways that I fell short. I always found something to be hard on for. I was always striving for

for perfection. And of course I'm human. I couldn't reach it. And so I always found, found the ways to pick myself apart and focus on those. But now that I use self-compassion, it's opened up a new sense of self that I'm at peace with my humanity. I'm at peace that I'm a human and I'm not full of perfection. I can now see my strengths and celebrate them. And I can also see my weaknesses and not get depressed about them. They don't sink me.

I'm human and I choose to celebrate that. I feel that I'm a better wife and a mom, a friend, and just all around person because I practice self-compassion. I found that people who are hard on others are usually even harder on themselves. So I've given myself permission to be more compassionate to myself. I've also gained or grown in compassion towards others. I see their humanity as well as my own. And I don't hold other people to an impossible standard either. Yeah. No, I love that. And it's.

It's crazy because you would think that if you're looking for all these weaknesses and trying to improve those, you would somehow become happier with yourself because you're getting rid of these things that kind of hurt you. And like you said, we can never achieve perfection. One more thing you fix or improve, there's going to be another one that shows up. But when you're practicing self-compassion, you become more happy with yourself and who you are. You have more self-love. And so...

logically, I think that was something for me that was really difficult for me to wrap my head around that like if I was kind of myself and if I love myself, I would, I don't want to say get closer to a point of perfection, but I would just be so much happier. And for me, the idea of perfection was happiness and loving life because I was like, that was something I just never experienced. And it was like, well, I don't know why that was what I pictured is that idea of perfection, but it wasn't ever like they have all these different things in life. It was like they loved their life. Yeah.

It was crazy to me that I was like, okay, if I accept these weaknesses, that makes me stronger. Like that didn't make sense logically, but in practice, it's so evident. And I don't know how to explain it other than that, that once you start loving these little bits of yourself, you feel stronger, you feel more complete, and you're able to give more of yourself to other people, and you begin to truly love your life. So yeah. I think part of it for me too was just loving where I was now.

regard like I didn't have to reach a certain point in order to love myself. I could love myself where I was, however I was. And it's actually self-compassion. They've done studies, how motivating self-compassion is because it's the right kind of motivating it. You're motivated because you love yourself, not because you need to reach a certain level of perfection or please somebody else or, you know, all these other different reasons to motivate yourself. You're motivated because you really want to do something and, and you're,

you're compassionate along the way. If you mess up, you know, on your way to your goal, you don't throw in the towel and say, oh my gosh, I'm such a terrible person. I can't do this. Why did I ever set this high goal? I should have known better. Instead you say, okay, that's a little setback. I, you know, had a really rough week. That's why I didn't reach my goals this week, but that's okay. I'm going to be aligned. I'm going to assess and then I'm going to go for it again.

And it's just the perfect motivator to know that you can be kind to yourself all along the way. And something that sticks out to me about that, I always talk about how the most difficult part is the beginning of recovery. It's accepting that there's something wrong. It's committing to wanting to change it for yourself. Like that is – and telling someone that is the hardest part and it really is downhill from there. It's not easy, but it's easier than realizing there's something wrong and saying that for the first time and being like, I care about myself enough to want to change this. And so –

The beautiful thing about mental health is once you start working on these little bits of yourself, whether it's your core beliefs, whether it's the self-compassion, whether it's vulnerability, making connections, finding joy through adventure, all these other little things fall into place because it's so connected. and you start to experience this happiness more because you care more about yourself and when you care more about yourself and you're stronger and feeling better overall you can help other people so your relationships go along with that and once you have these relationships you're being more vulnerable and so it's like kind of that's one of the great things about choosing to work on yourself is that it gets easier and it all falls into place it's

it's like a skill. Again, it's a muscle. You get better at it. It gets easier. And I love that. That's one of the most amazing things about mental health is that it's rewarding. It's not just like you're working on it because you have to or because there's a reward. And it's hard to see. And I never believed that I could be happier that treatment would work or that recovery was possible. But it is. And it's evident. And you feel it. And you can find it for sure. So yeah.

So lastly, I wanted to touch on coping. So when we touched base last week, we both agreed that coping and mental health are skills that can be improved. Your mind is a muscle and so is your mental health. So this is something that gets lost a lot of the time. There's a belief that once you reach happiness or once you're mentally healthy, you're done. Your journey's over and you've checked the box and that it'll just kind of stay that way, you know? And so this is not the case. The same way with when you're depressed, you are maintaining that depression with not

not choosing to do the opposite. So I wanted to ask you, how do you continue to grow mentally and challenge yourself to improve your mental fitness? Oh, every day. Every day I work on it. Every day I do something, whether that's journaling or just practicing some mindfulness for a few moments. Yeah. I love reading books and listening to podcasts like yours. There's so many things out there to help us. There's really endless resources, reading articles online, or there's even, I love, there's some Netflix documentaries that are pretty great. There's just so much out there that I try to do something every day to just focus on my value as a person. That's one of my core issues is that I've seen myself as unlovable

not worth it. If I can spend a few minutes doing some affirmations to remind myself that I am worth it and that I am valuable and lovable, then that kind of sets the tone for the day. If I have something that comes up where, you know, some negativity takes hold, maybe it's some body image things, then I'm able to identify it and stop myself and then remind myself, you know, how amazing my body is and how much,

It lets me experience in different things and I'm able to shift my mindset and just kind of get, make sure that I don't sink into a dark place again. Absolutely. Yeah. So every day, every day is something that I need to do. It's, it's, you're right. There's no finish line. Um, actually in my self-compassion book, my workbook that I have, I, I just say that it's starting you on your journey. You don't get a medal for finishing.
